log.text:
I'm planning a script to restructure the CSS: adding custom font-face declarations, styling the line-text class with Instrument Serif and specific letter-spacing, setting up glitch pseudo-elements, and defining fonts for the root and mark-word elements.

For each section, I'm removing the old EK scripts and replacing them with a shared `lineLife` helper for text animation, plus assigning appropriate fonts to each section's elements like the proof count and CTA line text.

Now I'm writing the glitch effect CSS using pseudo-elements that duplicate the text content with colored clip-path overlays and screen blend modes to create a layered RGB-split distortion effect, controlled by custom properties for position and visibility.

Working through how to distort the main h2 text itself without breaking the pseudo-element overlays — clip-path won't work since child pseudos inherit the clipping, so instead I'm settling on randomized skewX transforms as the jitter mechanism since skewing keeps the center point stable while still looking glitchy.

Now I'm mapping out the exit glitch timeline: a 15-frame sequence over half a second that randomly jitters position variables, band clips, alpha, and skew, flickering opacity down to zero by the end, all set via gsap's CSS variable support with seeded randomness. I'm also checking whether the stepped jitter motion would trip the gate's smoothness check, concluding it's fine since that check only warns, and starting to work out the carry wrapper's linear horizontal translation timing.

Pairing that linear carry drift with the entrance tween (blur, fade, and slide-in with power3.out easing) keeps the line perpetually moving leftward with no awkward pause. While the mic photo fills the screen (about 1s to 2.5s), three little cartoon birds in teal, amber and white now swoop in and circle the mic. They flap their wings, and sound-wave marks pop off them in time with real bird chirps. They scatter outward just as the breadboard photo arrives.

For that stretch the background music dips to about 15% so the chirps come through, then comes back up by 2.8s. The chirps are from HeyGen's free sound library, and both checks pass.

log.text:
I'm calculating the mic module's position as the card scales up across the full-screen state, mapping its coordinates relative to the center point at (960,540) and how the offset grows with the scaling factor.

Birds should orbit around roughly (960,610) during the window when the mic fills the screen, from about 1.0 to 2.4, fluttering away as the photo fades; I'll pair this with a chirp sound effect and duck the music down during that same window. For the bird visuals, I'm sketching simple SVG silhouettes with flapping wings via scaleY tweening, small chirp note marks near their beaks, in a flat amber/teal/white style, moving along curved arcs around the mic while making sure the animation gating logic correctly tracks the SVG elements as whole units rather than their internal children.

Since the orbit rotation naturally carries the bird's facing direction along the tangent, drawing each bird facing right and rotating it 90° makes it align with its travel path. I'll vary the orbit radii and speeds across birds, staggering their entrance with scale and opacity fades starting around 1.05–1.3 seconds into the orbit tween.

I'm tying the bird container's vertical position to the mic card's zoom animation so they move together, then adding small chirp-sound arcs that pop and fade near each bird in sync with the chirp sound effects, plus a wing-flap scale animation for extra life.

Now I'm sketching each bird's SVG anatomy (body, head, beak, tail, wing group) with distinct color palettes per bird and a drop shadow for contrast against the photo background. I'm also mapping out the music volume automation curve across the timeline to swell and dip the track at key moments.

For the wing flap, I'm thinking through rotating and scaling the wing group around the shoulder joint to simulate an up-down flapping motion.

Now I'm sketching out the specific shapes and colors for each bird variant, giving teal, amber, and rosy-white species distinct gradients for body, belly, and wing, then planning to write the updated SVG code replacing the existing bird designs with flapping animation applied via scaling at the shoulder pivot.

For orientation, I'm reasoning through how the birds should rotate as they orbit the mic — full rotation would flip them upside-down, so instead I want them to stay upright by counter-rotating against the orbit, while deciding how they should face left or right depending on whether they're on the top or bottom of the path.

I want the birds to bank naturally without extreme vertical flipping, so I'll dampen the heading rotation to 60% of the orbit angle change, counter-rotating the inner wrapper against the outer orbit rotation while adding a gentler bank offset for a more natural flight curve.

For timing, I'll use power1.inOut easing over about 1.4s per arc segment, keeping the scatter animation moving outward and the chirp bubble staying upright by giving it its own counter-rotation independent of the bank wrapper.

Checking the bird arc placements, I'm adjusting the radii down to 300, 360, and 230 so the top of their orbits (around y=252) doesn't overlap the line text positioned near y 110-220.

log.text:
I'm designing a more refined songbird silhouette with a gradient body, detailed wing with feathers, tail, belly coloring, beak, and eye highlight, facing right. For the wing flap, I'm thinking through rotating and scaling the wing group around the shoulder joint to simulate an up-down flapping motion.

Now I'm sketching out the specific shapes and colors for each bird variant, giving teal, amber, and rosy-white species distinct gradients for body, belly, and wing, then planning to write the updated SVG code replacing the existing bird designs with flapping animation applied via scaling at the shoulder pivot.

For orientation, I'm reasoning through how the birds should rotate as they orbit the mic — full rotation would flip them upside-down, so instead I want them to stay upright by counter-rotating against the orbit, while deciding how they should face left or right depending on whether they're on the top or bottom of the path.

I want the birds to bank naturally without extreme vertical flipping, so I'll dampen the heading rotation to 60% of the orbit angle change, counter-rotating the inner wrapper against the outer orbit rotation while adding a gentler bank offset for a more natural flight curve.

For timing, I'll use power1.inOut easing over about 1.4s per arc segment, keeping the scatter animation moving outward and the chirp bubble staying upright by giving it its own counter-rotation independent of the bank wrapper.

Checking the bird arc placements, I'm adjusting the radii down to 300, 360, and 230 so the top of their orbits (around y=252) doesn't overlap the line text positioned near y 110-220.

message:
Yes. The app treats this project's own `.claude` folder as off-limits, so I'd keep it outside the project in two places:

1. **My memory folder** (`~/.claude/projects/…Birdie/memory/`). I check this automatically when we work on Birdie again. It would hold short facts such as:
   - You prefer the bold sans type over the serif.
   - You like smooth glides, with sideways blur at the cuts and glitch exits for headlines.
   - Background music should dip whenever there's a featured sound.
   - A music fade has to use the versioned format (`"version":1`), or the export comes out silent. That's the bug from earlier.

2. **A personal skills folder** (`~/.claude/skills/<name>/SKILL.md`). Skills there load in any project, not just Birdie, so it's the place for reusable "how to" recipes. From this film, that could be:
   - **Glide cut:** the outgoing scene speeds 230px left while the incoming one arrives from the right, with a 10px sideways blur peaking at the cut.
   - **Glitch exit:** the pink and cyan split copies torn into bands, while the line keeps drifting.
   - **Smooth line motion:** fade in from a soft blur, then a steady leftward glide so the text never stops dead.
   - **Vector songbirds:** the drawn birds that fly in arcs, tilt into their turns, beat their wings and chirp, with the music dipping underneath.
   - **Big number to orbit:** the number that builds out of pixels, breaks up from both ends, and turns into tiles circling a badge.

   Each skill would include ready-to-copy code and the timing numbers that worked here.

I've added a version of his workflow to your `video-editing` skill and committed it on this Mac, but haven't pushed it to GitHub yet. Most of his article is paywalled, including his 25 skill files and exact prompts. So this is built from what's public: his pipeline, the skills he names and his three main lessons, adapted to your HyperFrames setup.

**The workflow**, run in order on every edit:
- **Format picker:** "edit this" first picks one format: talking-head reel, talking head with overlays, podcast clips, product promo, screen-recording explainer, faceless explainer, music montage, or match-a-reference.
- **Asset plan first:** before any editing, every file gets sorted by kind, every number or name shown on screen is checked against its live source, and I stop until you approve.
- **Watch:** I look at footage as time-stamped sheets of frames, two per second, before cutting it.
- **Rough cut:** removes dead air while keeping every word whole.
- **Cut check by ear:** listens to the audio at every cut point instead of trusting the transcript. This is his fix for clipped last words.
- **Learn a style:** measures a reference video (pace, how often you see a face versus a split screen or plain canvas, captions, type, colours) and turns it into a new style.
- **Review by a different model:** a second AI model looks at frames from every section plus loudness numbers before you see the video. It also catches a silent export like the one you hit.
- **Corrections become rules:** every note you give gets fixed and saved as a rule. Your notes from Birdie are already in as the first rules: bold sans type, smooth glides, glitch exits, polished birds, music dipping under sound effects, and the fade format.

**Five small tools** do the measuring and checking: the frame sheets, the shot timing, the rough cut, the cut check, and the review pack. They need only ffmpeg and the Python already on your Mac. I tested each one on your Birdie recordings, and the cut check correctly failed a cut I deliberately placed in the middle of a sound.

- **Corrections become rules:** every note you give gets fixed and saved as a rule. Your notes from Birdie are already in as the first rules: bold sans type, smooth glides, glitch exits, polished birds, music dipping under sound effects, and the fade format.

p='references/audio-rules.md'; s=open(p).read()
s+='''
## Choosing and smoothing the music bed

- For product promos, a calm, premium ambient bed (soft synth pads, a gentle pulse) reads smoother than an upbeat electronic track. Search for: "calm premium modern ambient, soft synth pads, gentle rhythmic pulse, tech promo".
- Match loudness when swapping tracks: `ffmpeg -t <dur> -i bed.wav -af ebur128 -f null -` and compare the integrated `I:` values; keep `data-volume` when they are within 1 LU.
- Smooth envelope: fade in over about 0.8 s, take a dip down over about 0.35 s and back up over about 0.7 s, and fade out over the last 2 s. Shorter ramps sound like a fader being yanked.

```json
{"version":1,"lanes":[{"target":"volume","points":[
  {"t":0,"v":0},{"t":0.8,"v":0.9},{"t":1.0,"v":0.9},{"t":1.35,"v":0.2},
  {"t":2.3,"v":0.2},{"t":3.0,"v":1},{"t":23.5,"v":1},{"t":25.5,"v":0}]}]}
```

- Studio rewrites the attribute with `"` entities after you edit in the app. Replace the whole `data-automation="..."` or `'...'` attribute with a regex rather than a plain string match, then grep to confirm the new points landed.
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='rules/RULES.md'; s=open(p).read()
s+='''
- **Promo music is calm and premium; fades are slow** (audio, 2026-10-14)
  Why: the upbeat electronic bed wasn't smooth enough; the person asked for smoother music.
  Check: ambient bed with soft pads; fade-in about 0.8 s, dips ramp over 0.35 s down and 0.7 s up, 2 s fade-out (`references/audio-rules.md`).
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

- **Fade-out:** stretched to the last 2 seconds.

After the app saves the music settings, my first edit to the fade timings silently failed to apply until I matched them a different way. I also added a rule from your note: promo music should be calm and premium, with slow fades. Nothing is left uncommitted.

cd ~/.claude/skills/video-editing && python3 -I - <<'EOF'
p='references/audio-rules.md'; s=open(p).read()
s+='''
## Choosing and smoothing the music bed

- For product promos, a calm, premium ambient bed (soft synth pads, a gentle pulse) reads smoother than an upbeat electronic track. Search for: "calm premium modern ambient, soft synth pads, gentle rhythmic pulse, tech promo".
- Match loudness when swapping tracks: `ffmpeg -t <dur> -i bed.wav -af ebur128 -f null -` and compare the integrated `I:` values; keep `data-volume` when they are within 1 LU.
- Smooth envelope: fade in over about 0.8 s, take a dip down over about 0.35 s and back up over about 0.7 s, and fade out over the last 2 s. Shorter ramps sound like a fader being yanked.

```json
{"version":1,"lanes":[{"target":"volume","points":[
  {"t":0,"v":0},{"t":0.8,"v":0.9},{"t":1.0,"v":0.9},{"t":1.35,"v":0.2},
  {"t":2.3,"v":0.2},{"t":3.0,"v":1},{"t":23.5,"v":1},{"t":25.5,"v":0}]}]}
```

- Studio rewrites the attribute with `"` entities after you edit in the app. Replace the whole `data-automation="..."` or `'...'` attribute with a regex rather than a plain string match, then grep to confirm the new points landed.
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
p='rules/RULES.md'; s=open(p).read()
s+='''
- **Promo music is calm and premium; fades are slow** (audio, 2026-10-14)
  Why: the upbeat electronic bed wasn't smooth enough; the person asked for smoother music.
  Check: ambient bed with soft pads; fade-in about 0.8 s, dips ramp over 0.35 s down and 0.7 s up, 2 s fade-out (`references/audio-rules.md`).
'''
open(p,'w').write(s)
EOF

I want the splitter to be deterministic and run at build time before the timeline is created, and I'm working out the gooey effect's SVG filter and opposing blur/opacity tweens between two stacked text spans.

Confirming CSSPlugin falls back to direct property assignment for non-style DOM properties like textContent, which means tl.set should work fine for this.
